# 01-mini-soc — Mini SOC on AWS

A minimal, real AWS detection lab: CloudTrail audit logging → encrypted S3 log
store → GuardDuty threat detection → Security Hub aggregation, with three
safe attack simulations (Stratus Red Team) and a Tier-1 triage workflow.

## Problem this solves

SOC analyst job postings ask for hands-on experience with SIEM-style
workflows — triaging alerts, reading audit logs, containing threats — that is
hard to get without working in a SOC. This project builds a working
mini-SOC in your own AWS account for ~$5–15/month, generates *real*
detections by safely simulating attacks, and documents the full
detect → triage → contain loop the way an employer expects to see it.

## 15-minute quickstart

> Requires: your **own** AWS account (never an employer's), Terraform ≥ 1.5,
> AWS CLI credentials, and the [Stratus Red Team](https://stratus-red-team.cloud/getting-started/)
> binary. All commands run from this directory.

```bash
# 1. Build the lab (~5 min)
cd terraform
terraform init
terraform plan        # read it — know what you're about to create
terraform apply       # type "yes"

# 2. Simulate an attack (~2 min)
stratus warmup   aws.exfiltration.s3-backdoor-bucket-policy
stratus detonate aws.exfiltration.s3-backdoor-bucket-policy

# 3. See the detection (~15-30 min for GuardDuty; CloudTrail is near-real-time)
#    GuardDuty console -> Findings, or:
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=PutBucketPolicy
#    Full scenario walkthrough: attack-runbook.md (Scenario 1)

# 4. Triage it like a Tier-1 analyst
#    Follow triage-guide.md -> Policy:S3/* row

# 5. Clean up the attack, then the lab
stratus cleanup aws.exfiltration.s3-backdoor-bucket-policy
stratus status        # must show COLD
cd terraform && terraform destroy   # type "yes" — destroys everything
```

Next: run scenarios 2 and 3 in `attack-runbook.md`, then write up one
detonation using `incident-reports/report-template.md`.

## What's in this project

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `terraform/main.tf` | The whole lab as code: VPC, encrypted S3 log bucket, multi-region CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub, least-privilege analyst IAM role. Every resource has a "why it exists" comment. |
| `architecture.md` | Data-flow diagram (mermaid) + design decisions (why multi-region trail, why encrypted log bucket, why no NAT gateway). |
| `attack-runbook.md` | 3 safe attack simulations with real [Stratus Red Team](https://stratus-red-team.cloud) technique IDs (verified against the official catalog): S3 exfiltration, IAM privilege escalation, EC2 mining-setup attempt. Includes exact commands, expected findings, and screenshot points. |
| `triage-guide.md` | GuardDuty finding types → triage steps: which logs to check, severity judgment, containment commands, escalation criteria. |
| `incident-reports/report-template.md` | Blank incident report template with per-field filling guide, plus a clearly marked **fictional** example (labeled EXAMPLE — DO NOT PRESENT AS REAL). Only real lab work goes in filled reports. |

## Skills demonstrated (mapped to SOC analyst JD keywords)

- **Security monitoring & triage** — worked GuardDuty finding queues, applied a
  severity model (Low/Medium/High/Critical), and made triage decisions.
- **Log analysis** — read CloudTrail events (`PutBucketPolicy`,
  `UpdateLoginProfile`, `RunInstances`) to answer "who did what, from where".
- **Threat detection engineering** — reasoned about sensor coverage: which
  attacks GuardDuty catches vs. which need CloudTrail analytics (scenarios 2–3).
- **Incident response** — containment playbooks: isolate EC2, revoke IAM
  credentials, revert S3 policies; escalation criteria for Tier-2 handoff.
- **Cloud security (AWS)** — GuardDuty, Security Hub (ASFF), CloudTrail,
  S3 security controls (SSE, block public access), IAM least privilege.
- **Infrastructure as code** — full lab in Terraform with cost controls.
- **Adversary emulation** — Stratus Red Team attack simulations mapped to
  MITRE ATT&CK tactics (Exfiltration, Privilege Escalation, Execution).
- **Documentation** — architecture decision records, runbooks, incident
  reports written for a reader who wasn't in the room.

## Cost & cleanup

- **Cost:** ~$5–15/month with the minimum configuration (see the cost
  breakdown at the top of `terraform/main.tf`). GuardDuty includes a 30-day
  free trial for new detectors. Set a billing alarm on the account.
- **Cleanup:** attacks first, infrastructure second —
  `stratus cleanup <technique-id>` (verify `stratus status` shows COLD),
  then `terraform destroy`. The S3 bucket uses `force_destroy` so the destroy
  does not fail on leftover log objects.
- **Never** run the attack simulations outside your own lab account.

# Architecture — 01-mini-soc ## Data-flow diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph AWS Account ["Lab AWS account (us-west-2)"] VPC["VPC 10.0.0.0/16
1 public subnet + IGW"] CT["CloudTrail
multi-region trail"] S3[("S3 log bucket
SSE-S3 + block public access")] GD["GuardDuty detector
S3 protection on"] SH["Security Hub"] VPC -->|"API activity on
all resources"| CT CT -->|"log files
(validated, hash-chained)"| S3 CT -->|"management events
as finding input"| GD S3 -->|"S3 data-plane
events"| GD GD -->|"findings (ASFF)"| SH end Analyst["SOC analyst
(least-privilege IAM role)"] GD -->|"finding queue
triage per triage-guide.md"| Analyst SH -->|"aggregated view"| Analyst S3 -->|"raw evidence
athena / console"| Analyst CT -->|"LookupEvents
who did what"| Analyst Attacker["Attack simulation
(Stratus Red Team)"] -.->|"detonate"| VPC ``` ## What each data flow carries 1. **VPC → CloudTrail.** Every AWS API call made against resources in the account (in *any* region, because the trail is multi-region) is recorded as a management event: who called it (`userIdentity`), what was called (`eventName`), from where (`sourceIPAddress`), and whether it succeeded (`errorCode`). This is the raw material for everything downstream. 2. **CloudTrail → S3.** Log files are delivered to the dedicated bucket every few minutes. With log file validation enabled, each file carries a digest, so tampering with a delivered log is detectable — the "can we trust the logs" control. 3. **CloudTrail → GuardDuty.** GuardDuty consumes the management-event stream as one of its finding inputs (alongside VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs when those exist). 4. **S3 → GuardDuty.** With S3 protection enabled, GuardDuty also monitors S3 data-plane activity (object-level access patterns) — this is what makes the S3 backdoor scenario (attack-runbook.md, scenario 1) detectable as `Policy:S3/BucketAnonymousAccessGranted`. 5. **GuardDuty → Security Hub.** Findings are forwarded in ASFF (AWS Security Finding Format), the standard schema. Security Hub is the aggregation point: one queue, one format, even after more sources (Inspector, Macie, Config) are added later. 6. **Everything → Analyst.** The analyst works from the least-privilege `soc-analyst` IAM role: findings from GuardDuty/Security Hub, raw evidence from the S3 bucket and CloudTrail LookupEvents. Triage procedure lives in `triage-guide.md`. ## Key design decisions ### Why a multi-region trail

# Attack Runbook — 01-mini-soc

> Three safe, self-contained attack simulations for the mini-SOC lab.
> Each one uses a real technique from the official
> [Stratus Red Team](https://stratus-red-team.cloud) catalog
> (DataDog open source, Apache 2.0). Technique IDs below were verified against
> the official catalog list page and the per-technique docs in
> [DataDog/stratus-red-team](https://github.com/DataDog/stratus-red-team)
> on 2026-10-14 — the exact verification pages are cited per scenario.
>
> **Safety rules (non-negotiable):**
> - Run these ONLY in your own lab AWS account — never in an employer's account.
> - Always `warmup` → `detonate` → verify findings → `cleanup`.
> - Confirm `stratus status` shows **COLD** for every technique before you run
>   `terraform destroy`.
> - All "expected findings" below are **expected, not observed** — they describe
>   what the lab is designed to produce, not incidents that have happened.

## Global prerequisites

- The lab from `terraform/` is applied (`terraform apply` succeeded).
- [Stratus Red Team](https://stratus-red-team.cloud/getting-started/) installed:
  `stratus version` works.
- AWS CLI credentials for the lab account with enough permission to let
  Stratus provision its prerequisites (the techniques below create an S3
  bucket, an IAM user, and an IAM role during warmup).
- Stratus and Terraform target the **same region** (`us-west-2` by default).
  GuardDuty and Security Hub are regional — findings appear in the region
  where the detonation happened.

Useful lifecycle commands (valid for every technique):

```bash
stratus warmup   <technique-id>   # provision prerequisites (idempotent)
stratus status                    # WARM = ready, COLD = cleaned up
stratus detonate <technique-id>   # run the attack simulation
stratus cleanup  <technique-id>   # tear down what warmup created
```

## Scenario 1 — S3 data-exfiltration simulation

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Technique ID | `aws.exfiltration.s3-backdoor-bucket-policy` |
| Official title | "Backdoor an S3 Bucket via its Bucket Policy" |
| MITRE ATT&CK mapping | Exfiltration (per official technique doc) |
| Verification source | Official catalog list: `https://stratus-red-team.cloud/attack-techniques/list/` · Technique doc: `https://github.com/DataDog/stratus-red-team/blob/main/docs/attack-techniques/AWS/aws.exfiltration.s3-backdoor-bucket-policy.md` |

### Objective
Simulate an attacker backdooring an S3 bucket policy so that an external,
attacker-controlled AWS account can read the bucket's objects. Practice
detecting cross-account access grants via CloudTrail and GuardDuty S3
protection, then triage it like a Tier-1 analyst.

### Prerequisites
- `stratus warmup` for this technique creates a fresh S3 bucket (prerequisite:
  permission to `s3:CreateBucket` and `s3:PutBucketPolicy` in the lab account).

# Incident Report Template

> **FILLING GUIDE — read before you write.** Each section below has 1–2 lines
> of guidance in *italics*. Delete the guidance lines when you fill the
> report. Write for a reader who was not in the room: a hiring manager or a
> Tier-2 analyst should understand what happened and what you did without
> asking you. Facts first, opinions labeled. Never invent details — if you do
> not know something, write "Unknown" and say how you would find out.
>
> **Honesty rule for this lab:** only document incidents you actually
> investigated here. Do not present lab exercises as production incidents and
> do not present the illustrative example at the bottom of this file as real.

---

# Incident Report: [SHORT TITLE]

- **Report ID:** `IR-YYYY-NNN`
- **Date opened:** YYYY-MM-DD
- **Date closed:** YYYY-MM-DD (or "Open")
- **Author:** [name / role]
- **Status:** Open / Contained / Closed
- **Severity:** Low / Medium / High / Critical (and one line justifying it)

## 1. Summary

*2–4 sentences: what happened, what was affected, and the outcome. Someone
should be able to read only this section and brief their manager.*

## 2. Timeline

*One row per event, in UTC. Include detection, triage actions, containment,
and recovery — with the evidence source for each row (e.g. "CloudTrail event
ID …", "GuardDuty finding …").*

| Time (UTC) | Event | Evidence / source |
|---|---|---|
| YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM | | |

## 3. Scope & Impact

*What was affected (resource ARNs, accounts, data classifications) and what
was NOT affected — stating the negative scope is as important as the
positive. Quantify where possible: number of resources, duration of exposure,
whether data was confirmed accessed vs. merely exposed.*

## 4. Root Cause

*The underlying reason the incident was possible — not just the trigger.
Distinguish "how the attacker got in" from "why the control failed".
If the root cause is still unconfirmed, label it "Hypothesis" and list what
would confirm or refute it.*

## 5. Containment & Eradication

*Exactly what you did to stop the bleeding (with timestamps), in order —
revoked keys, isolated instances, reverted policies. Then what you did to
remove the attacker's foothold entirely (deleted persistence, rotated all
affected credentials). Link the commands or console paths used.*

# =============================================================================
# 01-mini-soc — Terraform: minimal AWS detection lab
#
# WHAT THIS BUILDS
#   A small, interview-ready SOC lab: VPC + an encrypted S3 log bucket,
#   a multi-region CloudTrail writing to that bucket, a GuardDuty detector,
#   a Security Hub account, and a least-privilege IAM role for analysis.
#   Nothing here runs compute, so the lab is cheap to keep alive.
#
# COST (estimates, us-west-2, minimum configuration)
#   - VPC / subnet / internet gateway / route table ............ $0.00
#   - S3 log bucket (a few GB of CloudTrail logs) ............... ~$0.10–0.50/mo
#   - CloudTrail trail: first trail with management events ...... $0.00
#       (data events and CloudTrail Insights are NOT enabled on purpose —
#        they are the expensive parts)
#   - GuardDuty: 30-day free trial for new detectors ............ $0.00
#       After the trial, S3 + EC2 protection on a quiet lab runs
#       roughly $1–4/mo. Finding publishing frequency does not change cost.
#   - Security Hub (no default standards enabled, see below) ... ~$0–2/mo
#   - IAM role / policies ....................................... $0.00
#   TOTAL: roughly $5–15/month after any free-trial period.
#   Set a billing alarm. If you only need the lab for a weekend,
#   the honest answer is that it costs pennies.
#
# REQUIREMENTS
#   - Your OWN AWS account (never run this in an employer's account).
#   - Terraform >= 1.5 and AWS CLI credentials configured
#     (e.g. `aws sts get-caller-identity` succeeds).
#   - GuardDuty and Security Hub are REGIONAL services: the region you
#     choose here is the region your findings live in. Stratus Red Team
#     techniques must be detonated in the same region.
#
# LIFECYCLE
#   terraform init
#   terraform plan
#   terraform apply
#   # ... run detections ...
#   terraform destroy   # destroys everything; the S3 bucket is force_destroy
#                       # so the destroy does not fail on leftover log objects
# =============================================================================

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

variable "aws_region" {
  description = "AWS region for the lab. GuardDuty and Security Hub are regional, so findings live here."
  type        = string
  default     = "us-west-2"
}

variable "project_prefix" {
  description = "Prefix applied to all resource names so lab resources are easy to identify (and to nuke)."

# Triage Guide — GuardDuty findings in 01-mini-soc

> How a Tier-1 SOC analyst works a GuardDuty finding in this lab:
> **confirm → scope → contain → escalate.** Every finding below is a real
> GuardDuty finding type (see the
> [GuardDuty finding types documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_finding-types.html)).
> Severity numbers follow the GuardDuty scale: **Low 1.0–3.9, Medium 4.0–6.9,
> High 7.0–8.9, Critical 9.0–10.**

## The 5-minute triage loop (use for every finding)

1. **Read the finding, not just the title.** Open the finding detail: note the
   severity, the resource (instance ID / bucket / IAM principal), the
   `service.action` fields, and the first/last seen timestamps.
2. **Check CloudTrail first.** In CloudTrail Event history (or the S3 log
   bucket), look up the principal and API calls around the finding window.
   CloudTrail answers "who did what, from where" — GuardDuty only answers
   "something looks wrong".
3. **Decide severity for yourself.** GuardDuty's score is a starting point;
   adjust it with context: production vs. lab, known vs. unknown principal,
   single event vs. pattern, business hours vs. 3 AM.
4. **Contain if it is real** (commands in the playbooks below).
5. **Escalate** when the scope exceeds one resource, when you cannot confirm
   the principal's legitimacy, or when the severity is High/Critical.

## Finding-type quick reference

| Finding type | What it usually means | First logs to check | Severity guidance | Containment | Escalate when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Policy:S3/BucketAnonymousAccessGranted` | S3 bucket policy now allows public/anonymous access | CloudTrail `PutBucketPolicy` on the bucket; bucket policy JSON | Start **High** — public data exposure until proven otherwise | Revert/remove the offending policy statement immediately | Data was actually accessed (check S3 access logs), or the grant came from an unknown principal |
| `CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS` | EC2 instance querying domains linked to Bitcoin mining pools | VPC Flow Logs + DNS query logs for the instance; CloudTrail `RunInstances` (who launched it) | **High** — active resource abuse, real money burning | Stop the instance (`aws ec2 stop-instances`); if compromise is confirmed, isolate via quarantine security group | Multiple instances, or the launch principal is compromised |
| `Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity.B!DNS` | Instance talking to a known command-and-control domain | DNS logs; VPC Flow Logs (destinations, ports); CloudTrail for how the instance was launched | **High/Critical** — assume compromised until proven otherwise | Isolate the instance (remove all security groups / attach quarantine SG); snapshot EBS for forensics *before* terminating | Any lateral-movement indicators (new IAM activity, unusual API calls from the instance role) |
| `Trojan:EC2/DNSDataExfiltration` | DNS tunneling / data exfiltration over DNS | DNS query logs (query volume, entropy of subdomains); VPC Flow Logs | **High** — data may already be leaving | Isolate the instance; preserve DNS logs | Volume suggests bulk exfiltration, or sensitive-data stores are in scope |
| `UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce` | Repeated SSH login attempts against an instance | VPC Flow Logs (source IPs, port 22); instance auth logs (`/var/log/secure`) | **Medium** by itself; **High** if followed by a successful login | Block offending IPs at the security group / NACL; verify no successful logins | A login succeeded (check `Accepted` in auth logs), or attempts come from many sources (distributed) |
| `Impact:EC2/PortSweep` | Instance probing many ports on many hosts | VPC Flow Logs (destination port spread from one source) | **Medium–High** — reconnaissance, often pre-attack | Isolate the scanning instance if it is yours and unauthorized | The scanner is external and targeting you → escalate to IR; internal scanner → verify with the owner |
| `PrivilegeEscalation:IAMUser/AdministrativePermissions` | IAM user/role granted admin-level permissions | CloudTrail `AttachUserPolicy` / `AttachRolePolicy` / `CreatePolicyVersion` | **High** — privilege escalation in progress | Revoke the grant (detach policy / delete policy version); disable the principal's keys | Grant came from a compromised admin, or the principal is already using the permissions |
| `Persistence:IAMUser/NetworkPermissions` | IAM principal granted network-modifying permissions (persistence setup) | CloudTrail IAM policy-change events | **Medium–High** | Same as above: detach, rotate keys | Combined with other persistence signals (new users, new keys) |
| `UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/TorIPCaller` | IAM API calls originating from a Tor exit node | CloudTrail (source IP, user agent, API calls made) | **High** — legitimate users do not administer AWS over Tor | Revoke active sessions (`aws iam` key deactivation); force password + MFA reset | Any successful sensitive API call (IAM changes, data access) |

> `!` in a finding type (e.g. `BitcoinTool.B!DNS`) means the evidence came
> from DNS logs. No suffix = evidence from Flow Logs / CloudTrail.

## Containment playbooks (lab-safe commands)

### A compromised or abusive EC2 instance
```bash
# 1. Isolate: strip all security groups, attach a quarantine SG with no rules
aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --groups sg-0quarantine0000000

# 2. Preserve evidence BEFORE terminating: snapshot the root volume
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --description "forensic-snapshot $(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"

# 3. Stop billing / abuse
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0
```
Then: find the launch principal in CloudTrail (`RunInstances`), rotate any
credentials on that principal, and check whether the same AMI/key pair was
used elsewhere.
